script.opening: (Wary, arms folded, direct.) "I'll be honest with you — I've not bothered much with all this diabetes stuff. I can't read your leaflets and forms, and we move around a fair bit so I never see the same doctor twice. Last place made me feel like a nuisance. I'm only here 'cause the wife's worried. So don't just talk at me, alright?"

facts.text: If asked how he'd like to be addressed: "Patrick's fine."
"Kept going on about missed appointments. Gave me forms. Looked at me like I was trouble. So I stopped going." Letters go to old addresses.
"She thinks I'll end up like people she's seen — bad feet, bad eyes. She nags me." His uncle lost a leg to diabetes.

"On and off. When we move I run out and don't always get more." Metformin — took it most days until a month ago; ran out. Doesn't know the name, recognises "the big white ones". No other medicines. No allergies.

"Nothing that's stopped me." If asked specifically: thirsty, up at night to pass urine, tingling in his feet sometimes, a cut on his foot that was slow to heal last month (now healed). Eyesight blurry at times. Never had eye screening.
"I'd rather not get into that today." If returned to gently at the end: smokes 20 a day.
If asked: "Depends. Why?" — drives a van for landscaping and tarmac work; car licence only. Not on insulin or gliclazide.
Lives on a site with his wife and four children; moves around 3–4 times a year, often in the north-west. Lots of tea with sugar, white bread, takeaways on the road.
Has a smartphone; his daughter reads texts to him. "That'd help. I lose papers."

Guarded; tests whether he'll be judged. If the doctor makes a deal not to lecture: "Deal." If handed leaflets or lectured, shut down: "See, this is what I mean." Opens up when asked what matters to him: "Something simple I can actually do. And the wife off my back." Engaged by plain explanation of eyes and feet: "Nobody's told me that."

ice.ideas: "Diabetes care is forms and lectures — it's never been for me."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — being treated as trouble or a nuisance again; not being able to read; his wife's fear of feet and eyes (his uncle's leg).

cues: "Don't just talk at me." — needs partnership and plain speech.
"I can't read your leaflets." — avoid written information.
"The wife's worried." — ask what she is worried about.

checkpoints.text: Recognises the health INEQUALITY (Gypsy/Traveller communities have among the worst UK outcomes/shortest life expectancy) and prioritises BUILDING TRUST — acknowledging prior poor experiences, being respectful and non-judgemental, signalling partnership

Communicates WITHOUT relying on written material — plain verbal language, visual aids, teach-back, no jargon, repeated understanding checks — and offers an advocate if helpful (he speaks English; the barrier is literacy, not language)
Avoids ASSUMPTIONS/stereotyping — asks about and tailors to his actual circumstances, diet, beliefs and priorities, respecting autonomy and countering the sense of being judged

Co-creates a FLEXIBLE plan for a mobile life — a portable record/summary, how to access care when moving (NHS England registration principles: no proof of address needed, temporary residence up to 3 months, immediately necessary treatment anywhere; walk-in), and prioritising the FEW most important actions rather than an overwhelming standard pathway

Manages the diabetes PRAGMATICALLY — highest-impact achievable steps (key medication, concrete simple dietary changes, smoking, BP, essential complication screening: eyes/feet/renal, an individual HbA1c target per NICE NG28, and asks what he drives before any DVLA advice) with feasible monitoring and continuity workarounds
Earns trust through manner — warm, respectful, unhurried, explicitly non-judgemental — reading the wariness as a response to prior discrimination, and treats the wife’s worry as the opening
Checks understanding with teach-back throughout, shares decisions, and leaves him feeling respected and willing to return

Safety-nets and follows up: a realistic, written-light plan he can actually use, a portable record, clear next steps and how to access care wherever he is, prioritised review, and an open door — partnership and accessibility, not leaflets or "talking at" him

worked.txt: "Thank you for coming in — I know it took something to do that, especially if you’ve been made to feel a nuisance before. That’s not how this will go. We’ll sort this out together, at your pace, and I won’t just talk at you."

"Forget the leaflets — we’ll talk it through, and I’ll keep it plain. Stop me any time. And now and then I’ll ask you to tell it back to me — not to test you, just to check I’ve explained it properly. That fair?"

"Tell me about your day-to-day — what you eat, how you’re feeling, what gets in the way. I don’t want to assume anything; you know your life best, and we’ll fit the diabetes around it, not the other way round."

"Since you move about, let’s do two things: I’ll give you a simple card with your diagnosis and tablets on it, so any doctor anywhere can pick it up — you’re entitled to care wherever you are, and a practice can’t turn you away for not having a fixed address. And we’ll keep it simple: a couple of the most important things rather than a big list."

"If we just nail two things to start — taking this one tablet regularly, and getting your eyes and feet checked — that alone makes a real difference. We can build from there. What feels doable for you?"

"You can come back to me — or any practice when you’re moving — and you won’t get grief. If you get very thirsty, drowsy, or unwell, get seen urgently. Tell your wife we’ve made a start. I’m glad you came, and I mean that."

f.learning: This is a HEALTH-INEQUALITIES / health-literacy consultation. Gypsy/Traveller communities experience among the WORST health outcomes and shortest life expectancy in the UK (EHRC Research report 12, 2009), driven by discrimination, mistrust of services, low literacy, poor continuity from a mobile lifestyle, and access barriers — so the FIRST task is to BUILD TRUST: acknowledge prior poor experiences, be respectful and explicitly non-judgemental, thank him for coming, and signal genuine partnership, because without trust nothing else lands. Do NOT rely on written information: with low literacy, leaflets and forms are useless or alienating, so communicate verbally in plain language, use visual aids and TEACH-BACK, avoid jargon, check understanding repeatedly, and offer an advocate if helpful (for an English speaker with low literacy, an interpreter is not the need) — "talking at" him or handing over leaflets is precisely the failure to avoid. Practise cultural HUMILITY: do not stereotype or assume his diet, beliefs or willingness; ask, listen, and tailor to his circumstances and priorities, respecting his autonomy and actively countering the sense of being judged that drives disengagement. Co-create a REALISTIC, FLEXIBLE plan for a mobile life — a portable record/summary of diagnosis and medication, clarity that he is entitled to care anywhere (NHS England patient registration standard operating principles: registration without proof of address, temporary residence for up to 3 months, immediately necessary treatment; walk-in/urgent services) and how to access it when moving, and prioritisation of the FEW highest-impact achievable actions rather than an overwhelming standard pathway he cannot follow. Manage the diabetes pragmatically (key medication adherence, concrete simple dietary change, smoking, BP, and essential complication screening — eyes, feet per NICE NG19, renal — against an individual HbA1c target per NICE NG28) with feasible monitoring and continuity workarounds, asking what he drives before any DVLA advice. The hidden agenda is wariness rooted in discrimination and the practical realities of literacy and mobility, with the wife’s worry the opening — earn trust this visit, make care accessible and flexible, prioritise ruthlessly, and leave him respected and willing to return, since a single good experience can transform engagement.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE NG28 (type 2 diabetes in adults: management, updated February 2026) · [2] NICE NG19 (diabetic foot problems) · [3] NHS England, Patient registration standard operating principles for primary medical care · [4] Equality Act 2010 · [5] EHRC Research report 12, Inequalities experienced by Gypsy and Traveller communities (2009) · [6] DVLA Assessing fitness to drive (November 2025 edition)
knowledge.summary: This is a health-inequalities consultation. Earn trust, communicate without relying on writing, avoid assumptions, and agree a short, portable plan that survives moving on. Good diabetes care here means doing the few highest-value things reliably.

points.t: Gypsy and Traveller communities have some of the poorest health outcomes and lowest life expectancy in the UK, linked to discrimination, poor access, low literacy and broken continuity (EHRC 2009 [5]). Romany Gypsies and Irish Travellers are protected as ethnic groups under the Equality Act 2010 [4].

NHS England [3]: a practice cannot refuse registration for lack of proof of address, identity or immigration status. People staying in an area for up to 3 months can register as temporary residents, and anyone can get immediately necessary treatment. Tell him this plainly.

With low literacy, leaflets and forms exclude him. Use plain speech, pictures or phone photos, a chunk-and-check approach and teach-back. NICE NG28 [1] asks that structured education be accessible, taking account of culture, literacy and individual needs; ask what format would work for him.

NICE NG28 [1]: agree an individual HbA1c target. Typically 48 mmol/mol on lifestyle or a single drug not causing hypoglycaemia, 53 mmol/mol on a drug that can; intensify if 58 mmol/mol or above. Relax targets where the risks outweigh the benefits.

Agree two or three actions: take the key medicine regularly, get eyes and feet checked, one food or drink change he chooses. Annual foot risk assessment (NICE NG19 [2]) and retinal screening via the NHS Diabetic Eye Screening Programme can be done wherever he is registered.
A patient-held summary (diagnosis, medicines, latest results, allergies) or a photo on his phone lets any practice continue care. Offer to send summaries when he registers elsewhere.

DVLA [6]: Group 1 drivers on diet or tablets that don’t cause hypoglycaemia need not notify. Group 2 (lorry, bus) drivers treated with tablets that carry a hypoglycaemia risk (sulfonylureas or glinides) must notify. Ask what he drives before assuming either.
Marked thirst, passing a lot of urine, weight loss, vomiting, drowsiness or a foot wound that is red, hot or not healing — be seen that day, at any practice, urgent care centre or A&E.

dg.d: Open start; let him state his terms (“don’t talk at me”); acknowledged his past experience.
Explored moving, running out of tablets, his wife’s worry, literacy, driving and what care has felt like.
HbA1c, renal function and ACR, lipids, BP, foot risk assessment (NICE NG19), retinal screening, as feasible before he moves.
Considered non-adherence due to supply gaps versus progressive disease; complication risk; hypo risk if on sulfonylurea.
Screened symptomatic hyperglycaemia and foot complications; urgent symptoms named.
Explained type 2 diabetes and its complications in plain speech linked to what his wife has seen.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Prioritised three actions with his agreement; individualised HbA1c target (NICE NG28); portable record; right to register anywhere (NHS England).
Smoking offered respectfully; BP and cardiovascular risk included; DVLA advice after asking what he drives.
Checks booked before he moves; teach-back; same-day red flags; open door at any practice.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Followed the cues: being made to feel a nuisance, running out when moving, his wife’s worry about feet and eyes.
Idea: diabetes care is forms and lectures not meant for him. Concern: being told off and complications. Expectation: something simple.
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — being treated as trouble or a nuisance again; not being able to read; his wife's fear of feet and eyes (his uncle's leg) — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

The tablets and checks, yeah. Food — let me think on one thing and I’ll tell you at the check.
That’s fair — your choice. I’ll also make you a small card with your diagnosis, tablets and latest results, and you can photograph it on your phone. Show it at any practice and they can carry on.
That’d help. I lose papers.
Just so I know I’ve explained it well — not testing you — can you tell me what we’ve agreed?
Tablets every day, blood and feet and eyes checked, card on my phone, pick one food thing, and I can see any GP.

Perfect. If you ever get very thirsty, are passing lots of water, being sick, very drowsy, or you get a foot sore that’s red, hot or not healing, get seen that day — any surgery, urgent care or A&E. Can we book the checks this week, before you move on?

social.t: Frequent moves break recall systems. Plan care that goes with him: portable summary, longer supply where safe, repeat from any pharmacy or practice.
His wife’s worry brought him in. With his consent, she can be part of the plan.

legal.t: Romany Gypsies and Irish Travellers are protected ethnic groups. Services must make adjustments and not discriminate.
NHS England: practices cannot refuse registration for lack of proof of address or ID; temporary registration for stays up to 3 months; immediately necessary treatment for anyone.

Group 1 on diet or tablets not causing hypoglycaemia: no need to notify. Group 2 treated with tablets carrying hypoglycaemia risk (sulfonylureas or glinides): must notify (DVLA Assessing fitness to drive, November 2025).

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024): treat patients fairly and respectfully, without discrimination, and support them to be involved in decisions.
Check understanding with teach-back; offer verbal, visual or phone-based information.

community.t: Friends, Families and Travellers (national charity) offers health advocacy and help registering with GPs. Local inclusion health or Traveller liaison services where available.

playbook.diagnosis: Type 2 diabetes with poor control, driven mainly by access, continuity and literacy barriers rather than unwillingness.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Diabetes is too much sugar in the blood. Over years it damages small vessels in the eyes, feet and kidneys. Steady tablets and a couple of checks prevent most of that.”

management.reflectIce: “Your wife is worried about feet and eyes, so those are exactly the checks we’ll do first.”
management.psychosocial: No leaflets. A short, spoken plan; a card or phone photo; supply and registration that work when he moves.
sharedPlan: Daily medication with a practical supply plan
HbA1c, kidney tests, BP, foot check (NICE NG19) and eye screening before he moves
One lifestyle change he chooses; individual HbA1c target (NICE NG28)
safetyNet: Same-day care for marked thirst, vomiting, drowsiness or an unhealing foot sore — any practice, urgent care or A&E

pitfalls.intro: This station tests whether you can make care work for someone the system has let down. It is failed on manner, on written information, and on a plan that ignores his life.

items.fail: Opening with his HbA1c and missed appointments.
items.why: It repeats the judgement he described; trust is lost in the first minute.
items.fix: Thank him for coming and accept his terms. Ask what happened last time.

items.fail: Stereotyped questions or assumptions about his diet, work or beliefs.
items.why: Assumptions are discrimination; examiners mark them down in Relating to Others.
items.fix: Ask open questions and let him tell you about his life.

items.fail: A written plan, diet sheet or referral forms.
items.why: He has told you he can’t read them. The plan will fail.
items.fix: Spoken plan, a simple card or phone photo, teach-back.

items.fail: A full standard annual-review list with no priorities.
items.why: Too much means nothing gets done; the Tasks domain rewards a realistic plan.
items.fix: Agree two or three actions and book the checks before he moves on.

items.fail: No plan for continuity when he moves.
items.why: Supply gaps are the main driver of his poor control.
items.fix: Longer supply where safe, a portable record, and his right to register anywhere.

items.fail: “Do you understand?” as the only check.
items.why: People with low literacy often say yes to avoid embarrassment.
items.fix: “So I know I’ve explained it well, can you tell me what we agreed?”

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: This is a health-inequalities consultation. Earn trust, communicate without relying on writing, avoid assumptions, and agree a short, portable plan that survives moving on. Good diabetes care here means doing the few highest-value things reliably.

points.t: Gypsy and Traveller communities have some of the poorest health outcomes and lowest life expectancy in the UK, linked to discrimination, poor access, low literacy and broken continuity (EHRC 2009 [5]). Romany Gypsies and Irish Travellers are protected as ethnic groups under the Equality Act 2010 [4].

NHS England [3]: a practice cannot refuse registration for lack of proof of address, identity or immigration status. People staying in an area for up to 3 months can register as temporary residents, and anyone can get immediately necessary treatment. Tell him this plainly.

With low literacy, leaflets and forms exclude him. Use plain speech, pictures or phone photos, a chunk-and-check approach and teach-back. NICE NG28 [1] asks that structured education be accessible, taking account of culture, literacy and individual needs; ask what format would work for him.

NICE NG28 [1]: agree an individual HbA1c target. Typically 48 mmol/mol on lifestyle or a single drug not causing hypoglycaemia, 53 mmol/mol on a drug that can; intensify if 58 mmol/mol or above. Relax targets where the risks outweigh the benefits.

Agree two or three actions: take the key medicine regularly, get eyes and feet checked, one food or drink change he chooses. Annual foot risk assessment (NICE NG19 [2]) and retinal screening via the NHS Diabetic Eye Screening Programme can be done wherever he is registered.
A patient-held summary (diagnosis, medicines, latest results, allergies) or a photo on his phone lets any practice continue care. Offer to send summaries when he registers elsewhere.

DVLA [6]: Group 1 drivers on diet or tablets that don’t cause hypoglycaemia need not notify. Group 2 (lorry, bus) drivers treated with tablets that carry a hypoglycaemia risk (sulfonylureas or glinides) must notify. Ask what he drives before assuming either.
Marked thirst, passing a lot of urine, weight loss, vomiting, drowsiness or a foot wound that is red, hot or not healing — be seen that day, at any practice, urgent care centre or A&E.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open start; let him state his terms (“don’t talk at me”); acknowledged his past experience.
Explored moving, running out of tablets, his wife’s worry, literacy, driving and what care has felt like.
Followed the cues: being made to feel a nuisance, running out when moving, his wife’s worry about feet and eyes.
Idea: diabetes care is forms and lectures not meant for him. Concern: being told off and complications. Expectation: something simple.
HbA1c, renal function and ACR, lipids, BP, foot risk assessment (NICE NG19), retinal screening, as feasible before he moves.
Considered non-adherence due to supply gaps versus progressive disease; complication risk; hypo risk if on sulfonylurea.
Screened symptomatic hyperglycaemia and foot complications; urgent symptoms named.
Explained type 2 diabetes and its complications in plain speech linked to what his wife has seen.
Prioritised three actions with his agreement; individualised HbA1c target (NICE NG28); portable record; right to register anywhere (NHS England).
Smoking offered respectfully; BP and cardiovascular risk included; DVLA advice after asking what he drives.
Checks booked before he moves; teach-back; same-day red flags; open door at any practice.

social.t: Frequent moves break recall systems. Plan care that goes with him: portable summary, longer supply where safe, repeat from any pharmacy or practice.
His wife’s worry brought him in. With his consent, she can be part of the plan.

legal.t: Romany Gypsies and Irish Travellers are protected ethnic groups. Services must make adjustments and not discriminate.
NHS England: practices cannot refuse registration for lack of proof of address or ID; temporary registration for stays up to 3 months; immediately necessary treatment for anyone.

Group 1 on diet or tablets not causing hypoglycaemia: no need to notify. Group 2 treated with tablets carrying hypoglycaemia risk (sulfonylureas or glinides): must notify (DVLA Assessing fitness to drive, November 2025).

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024): treat patients fairly and respectfully, without discrimination, and support them to be involved in decisions.
Check understanding with teach-back; offer verbal, visual or phone-based information.

community.t: Friends, Families and Travellers (national charity) offers health advocacy and help registering with GPs. Local inclusion health or Traveller liaison services where available.

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Type 2 diabetes with poor control, driven mainly by access, continuity and literacy barriers rather than unwillingness.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Diabetes is too much sugar in the blood. Over years it damages small vessels in the eyes, feet and kidneys. Steady tablets and a couple of checks prevent most of that.”

management.reflectIce: “Your wife is worried about feet and eyes, so those are exactly the checks we’ll do first.”
management.psychosocial: No leaflets. A short, spoken plan; a card or phone photo; supply and registration that work when he moves.
sharedPlan: Daily medication with a practical supply plan
HbA1c, kidney tests, BP, foot check (NICE NG19) and eye screening before he moves
One lifestyle change he chooses; individual HbA1c target (NICE NG28)
safetyNet: Same-day care for marked thirst, vomiting, drowsiness or an unhealing foot sore — any practice, urgent care or A&E
He can register anywhere, including as a temporary resident

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests whether you can make care work for someone the system has let down. It is failed on manner, on written information, and on a plan that ignores his life.

items.fail: Opening with his HbA1c and missed appointments.
items.why: It repeats the judgement he described; trust is lost in the first minute.
items.fix: Thank him for coming and accept his terms. Ask what happened last time.

items.fail: Stereotyped questions or assumptions about his diet, work or beliefs.
items.why: Assumptions are discrimination; examiners mark them down in Relating to Others.
items.fix: Ask open questions and let him tell you about his life.

items.fail: A written plan, diet sheet or referral forms.
items.why: He has told you he can’t read them. The plan will fail.
items.fix: Spoken plan, a simple card or phone photo, teach-back.

items.fail: A full standard annual-review list with no priorities.
items.why: Too much means nothing gets done; the Tasks domain rewards a realistic plan.
items.fix: Agree two or three actions and book the checks before he moves on.

items.fail: No plan for continuity when he moves.
items.why: Supply gaps are the main driver of his poor control.
items.fix: Longer supply where safe, a portable record, and his right to register anywhere.

items.fail: “Do you understand?” as the only check.
items.why: People with low literacy often say yes to avoid embarrassment.
items.fix: “So I know I’ve explained it well, can you tell me what we agreed?”
